MAGNA CHARTA .
THE GREAT CHARTER ,
(TRANSLATED AS IN THE STATUTES AT LARGE ),
MADE IN THE NINTH YEAR OF KING HENRY THE THIRD , AND CONFIRMED
BY KING EDWARD THE FIRST , IN THE FIVE -AND-
TWENTIETH YEAR OF HIS REIGN .
EDWARD ,by the grace of God ,King of England ,Lord of Ireland,and Duke of Guyan :
to allarchbishops , & c. We have seen the Great Charter of the Lord Henry , sometimes
King of England , our father, of the Libertiesof England , in these words :
" HENRY ,by the grace of God ,King of England ,Lord of Ireland,Duke of Normandy
and Guyan , and Earl of Anjou : to allarchbishops , bishops , abbots , priors, earls, barons ,
sheriffs, provosts, and officers, and to all bailiffsand other our faithful subjects, which
shall see this present Charter , greeting : Know ye that We , unto the honour of Almighty
God ,and forthe salvation of the soulsof our progenitors and successors,kings of England ,
to the advancement of Holy Church and amendment of our realm ,of our mere and free
will have given and granted to allarchbishops , bishops , abbots , priors, earls, barons , and
to all freemen of thisour realm,these libertiesfollowing,to be kept in our kingdom of
England forever."
CHAPTER I.
FIRST , we have granted to God , and by this our present Charter have confirmed for us
and our heirs forever,that the Church of England shallbe free,and shallhave allher whole
rights and libertiesinviolable. We have granted also, and given to all the freemen of
our realm , for us and our heirs forever, these liberties, under written, to have and to hold
to them and their heirs, of us and our heirs forever.
CHAPTER II .
If any of our earls,or barons , or others, who hold of us in chief by military service,
shall die, and at the time of his death his heir shall be of fullage , and owes a relief,he
shallhave his inheritance by the ancient relief; that is to say,the heir or heirs of an earl,
for a whole earldom ,by a hundred pounds ; the heir or heirs of a baron , for a whole barony ,
by a hundred pounds ; the heir or heirs of a knight ,for a whole knight's fee,by a hundred
shillingsat most ; and whoever oweth lessshallgive less,accordingto the ancientcustom
of fees .
CHAPTER III.
But if the heir of any such shall be under age and shall be in ward when he comes of
age ,he shall have his inheritance without reliefand without fine.
CHAPTER IV .
The keeperof the land of such an heir being under age,shalltake of the land of the
heir none but reasonable issues,reasonable customs , and reasonable services,and that with-
out destruction and waste of his men and his goods ; and if we commit the custody of any
such lands to the sheriff,or any other who isanswerable to us forthe issuesof the land, and
he shall make destruction and waste of the lands which he hath in custody , we will take
of him amends ,and theland shallbe committed to two lawfuland discreetmen of thatfee,

CHAPTER VII .
A widow , after the death of her husband , shall forthwith and without difficultyhave

not marry without our assent, if she holds of us ; or without the consent of the lord of
whom she holds, if she hold of another .

ARTICLE II.-
§ 1. 1. President- term of office. The executivepower shallbe vestedin a President
of the United States of America . He shall hold his officeduring the term of four years,
and ,together with the Vice -President, chosen for the same term , be elected as follows :
2. Presidentialelectors. Each State shall appoint , in such manner as the Legislature
thereof may direct, a number of electors, equal to the whole number of Senators and
Representatives to which the State may be entitled in the Congress ; but no Senator or
Representative,or person holding an officeof trust or profitunder the United States, shall
be appointed an elector.
[3. The electorsshall meet in their respectiveStates, and vote by ballotfor two persons,
of whom one at least shall not be an inhabitant of the same State with themselves ; and
they shallmake a listof allthe persons voted for,and of the number of votes foreach ; which
listthey shall sign and certify, and transmit , sealed, to the Seat of the Government of the
United States,directed to the President of the Senate . The President of the Senate shall,
in the presence of the Senate and House of Representatives , open all the certificates, and
the votes shall then be counted . The person having the greatest number of votes shallbe
thePresident,if such number be a majorityof the whole number of electorsappointed;
and ifthere be more than one who have such majority,and have an equal number of
votes, then the House of Representatives shall immediately chuse , by ballot, one of them
forPresident; and ifno personhave a majority,then,from the fivehigheston the list,the
said House shall, in like manner , chuse the President . But , in chusing the President,
thevotesshallbe taken by States,the representationfrom each Statehaving one vote; a
quorum for this purpose shall consist of a member or members from two -thirds of the
States,and a majorityof allthe Statesshallbe necessaryto a choice. In everycase,after
the choice of the President ,the person having the greatest number of votes of the electors,
shallbe the Vice -President. But if there should remain two or more who have equal votes,
theSenate shallchuse from them , by ballot, the Vice-President]. (See as substitutefor
clausein brackets,Article12.)
4. Congress to fix time of meeting. The Congress may determine the time of chusing
the electors, and the day on which they shall give their votes ; which day shall be the
same throughout the United States.
5. Qualificationsof President. No person except a natural born citizen, or a citizen
of the United States, at the time of the adoption of this Constitution, shall be eligibleto
the officeof President ; neither shall any person be eligibleto that officewho shall not
have attained to the age of thirty-five years , and been fourteen years a resident within
the United States .
6. Provision in event of President'sdeath. In case of the removal of the President from
office, or of his death, resignationor inabilityto discharge the powers and dutiesof
thesaid office,the same shalldevolve on the Vice-President, and the Congress may by
law provide for the case of removal , death , resignation or inability, both of the President
and Vice-President , declaring what officershall then act as President , and such officer
shallactaccordingly,untilthe disabilitybe removed ,or a Presidentshallbe elected.

vices,a compensation ,which shall neither be increased nor diminished during the period
forwhich he shall have been elected,and he shall not receive within that period any other
emolument from the United States, or any of them .

ingoath or affirmation :
" I do solemnly swear (or affirm) that I will faithfullyexecute the officeof Presi-

classification.summary: This section of the Kentucky Constitution, specifically Article VII concerning slaves, outlines the powers of the General Assembly regarding emancipation and the treatment of slaves. It states the Assembly cannot emancipate slaves without owner consent or compensation, can allow slave owners to emancipate slaves while protecting creditors and preventing public charge, and can prevent slaves from being brought into the state as merchandise or from foreign countries. It also mandates laws for humane treatment, clothing, provisions, and protection from injury, with provisions for selling slaves if owners fail to comply. Section 2 addresses the prosecution of slaves for felony, stating no grand jury inquest is necessary but requiring an impartial trial by a petit jury.
classification.reasoning: The statute explicitly discusses 'slaves' and the legal framework surrounding their ownership, emancipation, and treatment. While it doesn't use terms like 'Black' or 'Negro,' the historical context of slavery in the United States, particularly during the period leading up to and following the Civil War, makes it clear that this legislation is directly related to the subjugation of enslaved people, who were overwhelmingly of African descent. Article VII, 'Concerning Slaves,' is a direct indicator of racial control and subjugation, fitting the criteria for Jim Crow-era legislation, even if it predates the formal 'Jim Crow' laws by a few decades, as it establishes the legal basis for racialized control over a population group. The explicit mention of 'slaves' and the detailed regulations concerning their status and treatment by owners, along with the limitations on emancipation, clearly mark this as a statute with a direct racial dimension. classification.title: PRESENT CONSTITUTION COMMONWEALTH OF KENTUCKY . [§ 11 Bill ofRights.
classification.summary: This section of the Kentucky Constitution outlines the rights of an accused person in criminal cases, including the right to counsel, to know the accusation, to confront witnesses, to compel witnesses, to not incriminate oneself, and to a speedy public trial by an impartial jury. It also allows for a change of venue under certain conditions. The text includes annotations and case law related to these rights.
classification.reasoning: The provided text is from the Bill of Rights section of the Kentucky Constitution. It details fundamental legal rights for individuals accused of crimes. There is no mention of race, nor are there any provisions that implicitly or explicitly discriminate based on race. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law.

§ 12-13] PRESENT CONSTITUTION COMMONWEALTH OF KENTUCKY .
Bill ofRights.
§ 12. Chargeofcrime- howpreferred. No person, for an indictableoffense,
shall be proceeded against criminally by information, except in cases
arisingin the land or naval forces, or in the militia, when in actual
servicein time of war or public danger, or by leave of court for oppres-
sion or misdemeanor in office.
§ 13. Jeopardy- propertynot to be taken without compensation. No person
shall, for the same offense, be twice put in jeopardy of his lifeor limb,
nor shallany man's property be taken or applied to public use without
the consent of his representatives, and without just compensation being
previouslymade to him . (See sec. 242, Con .)
(12) Ticket system of admission to court
room during a trial, to prevent the room
from being overcrowded , does not, under
proper regulations, deprive the accused of
his right to a public trial. Jackson v . Com .,
100 Ky ., 239; 18 R., 795.
(13) Wills- probating by order of Appel-
late Court . Order directing will to be pro-
bated contrary to the findingof the jury.
Wells v. Lochnane , 9 Bush , 547.
(14 ) Witnesses . When the accused has
been awarded compulsory process for his
witnesses and reasonable time to procure
their attendance, he is not entitledto a con-
tinuance if the Commonwealth will admit
that the absent witness, if present, would
testify to the facts stated in the affidavit
for a continuance. Adkins v . Com ., 98 Ky .,
539 ; 17 R., 1091; and see notes to sec. 189
(Carroll's), Criminal Code .
§ 12. (1) Application of section. This sec-
tion applies to crimes and misdemeanors
prosecuted by the Government , for public
redress, and not to any proceeding for the
benefitof the party injured by the illegal
act. Harrisonv. Chiles, 3 Litt., 194.
(2) Betting on electionswas never a crime
or an indictableoffenseat the common law,
and does not come within the meaning of
this section. Com . v . Avery , 14 Bush , 625.
(3) Misdemeanors created by statute may
be prosecutedby warrant. Lowry v. Com .,
18 R. , 481 .
(4) Municipal corporationsviolation of
ordinances. The Legislature may give to a
citythe power to proceedby warrant against
violators of its ordinances, which are pun-
ishable by fine. Such proceedings are penal
rather than criminal. Williamson v . Com .,
4 B. M. , 146.
(5) Proceedings for contempt . No indict-
ment necessary. Arnold v . Com ., 80 Ky .,300 ;
3 R. , 784 .
TWICE IN JEOPARDY .
§ 13. (1) Definitionof twice in jeopardy.
"A personisin legaljeopardywhen he isput
upon trialbefore a court of competent juris-
diction upon indictment or information which
is sufficient in form and substance to sustain
a conviction, and a jury has been charged
with his deliverance, and a jury is said to be
thus charged when they have been empaneled
and sworn ." Williams v . Com ., 78 Ky ., 93 ;
Gaskins v . Com ., 97 Ky ., 494 ; 17 R., 352 ;
Huff v . Com ., 19 R., 1064 ; and see notes to
sec. 176 (Carroll's), Criminal Code .
(2) Discharge of jury because of their fail-
ure to agree does not operate as an acquittal
or bar to another trial. Yarbrough v . Com .,
89 Ky ., 151. But dischargeof juror, or jury,
after they have been sworn against objection
of accused,save in caseof necessity,operates
as an acquittal,and bars a retrial. Robinson
v. Com ., 88 Ky ., 386 ; 10 R., 972 ; Williams v .
Com .,78 Ky .,93 ; Coliver v . Com .,90 Ky .,262 ;
12 R. , 160 ; O'Brian v . Com ., 9 Bush , 333 .
(3) Dismissal of indictment, with the con-
sent of the court,even after a jury was sworn
to try the case, is no bar to another indict-
ment . Wilson v . Com ., 3 Bush , 105. But in
Williams v.Com .,78 Ky .,93,the dismissalof
an indictmentagainstthedefendant'sprotest,
afterthe jury had been sworn, and the de-
fendant had pleaded and part of the evidence
heard , was held to bar a prosecution under a
new indictment. See preceding note .
(4) Double punishment. The Legislature
has the power to inflictmore than one pen-
alty for the same offense, providedthe pen-
alty does not affect life or limb . Com . v .
Gilbert,6 J. J. M.,184. This power seems to
have been questioned in Chiles v . Drake , 2
Met ., 146, where itwas held that a law au-
thorizinga civilactionby the representative
of one killedby the willfulneglectof an-
other was not liableto condemnation , though
the defendant be liable to an indictment for
the same offense. In Com . v . Avery , 14 Bush ,
625, itwas held that punishinga defendant
forbettingon an election,and alsoin a civil
action, is not punishinghim twice.
(5) Insufficientindictment. A conviction
on an insufficientindictment, and therefore
set aside, is not a bar to another prosecution.
Mount v .Com ., 2 Duv .,93.

classification.title: Bill of Rights - Sections 12 and 13
classification.summary: Section 12 outlines the preferred methods for charging crimes, generally requiring indictment for indictable offenses except in specific military or official misconduct cases. Section 13 addresses double jeopardy, stating no person shall be twice put in jeopardy for the same offense, and prohibits taking property for public use without consent and just compensation. The text also includes annotations and case law related to these sections.
classification.reasoning: The provided text contains sections 12 and 13 of the Bill of Rights of the Commonwealth of Kentucky Constitution. These sections deal with fundamental legal protections such as the process for preferring charges against an accused person and the prohibition against double jeopardy. There is no mention of race, nor any implicit or explicit racial discrimination within these specific constitutional provisions or the accompanying case law annotations. Therefore, this statute is not a Jim Crow law.

It details that money can only be drawn from the treasury through appropriations, requires annual publication of financial statements, allows the General Assembly to direct how suits against the Commonwealth can be brought, prescribes the manner of administering oaths, states that pre-existing Virginia laws remain in force unless altered or repealed, and mandates that civil officers reside within their respective districts, counties, cities, or towns.
classification.reasoning: The provided text is from the Constitution of the Commonwealth of Kentucky. It details general provisions regarding state finances, legal proceedings against the state, oaths, historical laws, and officer residency. There is no mention of race, nor are there any provisions that implicitly suggest racial segregation or discrimination. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law.

classification.summary: This statute outlines two distinct legal provisions. The first, § 7, details the right of a property owner to recover damages if their property is distrained or attached without good cause. It specifies that malice does not need to be proven and allows for recovery of damages for wrongful seizure, sale, and legal costs, including attorney fees. The second, § 8, addresses a city's liability for damages to property (churches, dwellings, businesses, transportation infrastructure, etc.) caused by riots or tumultuous assemblages. This liability is contingent on the city authorities having the ability to prevent the damage and having had notice of the impending or ongoing riot. Individuals who contributed to the riot or failed to prevent it cannot maintain such an action.

classification.summary: This statute outlines measures for controlling and eradicating pleuro-pneumonia in cattle. It grants powers to juries and courts in trials related to violations of animal disease statutes, allows for the appropriation of funds to purchase and destroy exposed cattle, sets compensation limits for killed cattle, and enables the establishment of quarantines against cattle from other states or countries. It also mandates confinement of diseased animals and penalizes owners who allow them to run at large.
classification.reasoning: The statute deals with animal infectious diseases, specifically pleuro-pneumonia in cattle. It outlines procedures for controlling the spread of the disease, including destruction of infected animals, compensation, and quarantine measures. There is no mention of race or any discriminatory provisions targeting specific racial groups. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law.

classification.title: ASSIGNMENTS - VOLUNTARY
classification.summary: This statute, enacted in 1894 and appearing in the 1903 Kentucky Statutes, outlines the rules for voluntary assignments made by debtors for the benefit of their creditors. It specifies that such assignments are for the benefit of all creditors proportionally, after expenses. It also details how liens on property are handled, prioritizing lienholders and allowing them to claim any remaining debt from the general assets. Additionally, it establishes that debts owed by the assignor in fiduciary capacities (guardian, committee, trustee, personal representative) are to be paid in full before general creditors receive anything. The annotations discuss various legal interpretations and case law related to assignments, attachments, and assignee compensation.

It outlines the distribution of assets, prioritization of liens, and preferred debts. There is no mention of race, nor are there any provisions that implicitly or explicitly discriminate based on race. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law. The document type is identified as 'session_laws' because it is presented as an 'Act of March 16, 1894' and is part of a compilation of statutes from a specific year.

classification.summary: This statute establishes a board to regulate the practice of barbering. It outlines requirements for barbers, including age, moral character, freedom from contagious diseases, and apprenticeship or study duration. It also details the board's compensation, reporting duties, examination procedures, and fees for certificates of registration. The statute aims to ensure sanitary conditions in barber shops and professional standards for barbers.
classification.reasoning: The statute focuses on regulating the barbering profession, establishing standards for practitioners and sanitary conditions in shops. There is no mention of race, nor are there any provisions that implicitly or explicitly create racial segregation or discrimination. The requirements are applied generally to all individuals seeking to practice barbering. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law.

There is no mention of race, nor are there any provisions that implicitly suggest racial segregation or discrimination. The requirements apply to all individuals seeking to practice barbering, regardless of race. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law.

The bonds are negotiable and payable in Kentucky or New York. The Sinking Fund Commissioners are responsible for selling the bonds to the highest bidder, with a minimum sale price of par value plus accumulated interest.

classification.title: Kentucky Statutes 1903, Chapter 16, Section 284-9: Charitable Institutions - Deaf Mutes
classification.summary: This statute mandates the admission of colored deaf and dumb pupils into the institution on the same terms as white pupils, providing equal per capita support. It also appropriates funds for a separate colored department, but crucially states that both races shall be under the same management and superintendent, with the colored department subject to the control of the board overseeing the white institution. This establishes a segregated but centrally controlled educational system for deaf and dumb individuals based on race.
classification.reasoning: The statute explicitly mentions 'colored deaf and dumb' and 'white deaf and dumb,' indicating a racial classification. While it states equal terms and per capita support, the provision for a 'colored department' under the same management and superintendent as the white institution, and subject to the same board, points to a system of racial segregation within the educational institution. This is characteristic of Jim Crow laws, which often mandated separate but unequal facilities or systems, even when superficially appearing equal. The explicit mention of race and the establishment of separate, though managed together, departments for different racial groups makes this a Jim Crow law. The confidence is high due to the explicit racial language and the nature of the segregation described.

classification.summary: This statute regulates the importation of dependent children into Kentucky. It requires individuals, corporations, associations, or institutions to provide a bond of ten thousand dollars to the county judge. This bond ensures that no incorrigible, unsound, or diseased children are brought into the state. It also mandates reporting the child's placement details to the Kentucky Children's Home Society and requires the removal of children who become a public charge or are convicted of a crime within five years of arrival. Failure to comply results in a forfeiture of one thousand dollars.
classification.reasoning: The statute focuses on the regulation of dependent children being brought into the state for placement. It outlines conditions and financial guarantees to prevent the state from becoming burdened by children with specific issues (incorrigibility, mental/physical unsoundness, contagious diseases) or those who become a public charge or commit crimes. There is no mention of race, nor are there any provisions that implicitly target or discriminate against a specific racial group. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law.

classification.title: Claims Upon the Treasury - Officers, Generally
classification.summary: This section details the fees and allowances for various judicial and law enforcement officers in Kentucky for services rendered in felony cases and examining courts. It specifies per diem rates for judges and Commonwealth's Attorneys, fees for magistrates holding examining courts, and payments for sheriffs, constables, coroners, marshals, and policemen for apprehending felons, executing summonses, conveying prisoners, attending circuit court, summoning juries, and executing contempt processes. It also includes provisions regarding the filing of affidavits before claims are allowed and notes on specific court cases and prior acts.
classification.reasoning: The provided statute text details the financial compensation and procedural requirements for various legal officers in Kentucky when handling felony cases and examining courts. It outlines specific fees for services such as apprehending suspects, executing warrants, and attending court. There is no mention of race, nor are there any provisions that implicitly or explicitly discriminate based on race. The statute appears to be a general administrative and financial regulation for the justice system. Therefore, it is classified as 'no' for Jim Crow, with a high confidence, and the category is 'other' as it doesn't fit the specific Jim Crow categories. The document type is 'codes' as it is presented as part of the Kentucky Statutes 1903.

classification.summary: This statute outlines the fees and allowances for various court officers in Kentucky, including circuit clerks, jailers, sheriffs, and elisors. It details specific amounts for tasks such as certifying juror lists, excusing jurors, summoning jurors, imprisoning and releasing prisoners, keeping and dieting prisoners, putting prisoners in irons, and attending court. § 470. (1) Construction. The statute applies

withinthe statute. Berry v.Graddy, 1 Met .,
553 .

or borrowed money under a verbal contract
to return property or pay money in three
years or longer, an action may be maintained
on the implied promise created by law.
Montague v. Garnett,3 Bush,297; and under
a contract for personal services, within the

quantum meruit . Kleeman v . Collins, 9 Bush ,
460 ; Myer v . Korb , 21 R., 163.

classification.title: Contracts
classification.summary: This section of the Kentucky Statutes from 1903 outlines rules regarding contracts, specifically addressing the necessity of seals, the impeachment of consideration, the verification of denials, and the assignability of bonds, bills, and notes. It clarifies that seals are generally not required for deeds or other writings, and that unsealed writings have the same legal standing as sealed ones. The statute also details how the consideration of a writing can be challenged and how the execution of a writing must be denied through a verified pleading. Furthermore, it explains the assignability of bonds, bills, and notes, noting that such assignments generally do not impair the defendant's right to defenses, discounts, or offsets that they could have used against the original obligee or an intermediate assignor before notice of the assignment. Special provisions are made for notes payable and discounted at banks, which are placed on the footing of bills of exchange, limiting defenses available against assignees.

classification.title: Railroad Commission - Jurisdiction and Prosecution
classification.summary: This statute outlines the jurisdiction of courts for offenses against railroad companies and their employees, specifying that circuit courts in counties through which the railroad operates, as well as the Franklin circuit court, have jurisdiction over offenses against the company. It also details that the circuit court of the county where an officer, agent, or employee commits an offense has jurisdiction over prosecutions against that individual. Prosecutions are to be by indictment and must be commenced within two years. The statute also describes the establishment and duties of the Railroad Commission, including its composition, powers, and the salaries and expenses of its members and secretary.

classification.title: Railroad Commission - Reporting Requirements
classification.summary: This statute outlines the reporting requirements for railroad companies to the Railroad Commission. It details the specific financial and operational data that must be submitted annually, including miles run by passenger and freight trains, freight tonnage, monthly earnings, expenses for various operational categories, and details about freight transportation companies operating on their lines. It also mandates the Commission to examine through freight rates from out-of-state points to in-state points and to appeal to the Interstate Commerce Commission if rates are found to be excessive, unreasonable, or discriminatory.

It focuses on financial and operational data and the regulation of freight rates, particularly those involving interstate commerce. the partiesto such action, proceeding or prosecution may make , after

record may not discloseany error committed

Massie v . Com ., 93 Ky ., 588 ; 14 R., 564.
(4) Objection when to be made . The ob-
jectionto the trialjudge, to be available,
must be made before an appearance to the
merits of the action, or the submission of pre-
liminary motions by eitherparty preparatory

based upon facts discovered since the issue
was made . Vance v . Field, 89 Ky ., 178; 11

(5) Objection to specialjudge must be made
in the circuitcourt, otherwise it will not be
available in the court of appeals. Vandever

(6) Presumption in favor of qualifications.
When a pro tempore judge has been elected,

Cotton v . Wolf , 14 Bush , 238 .
(7) Provision for judge of another district

viding that where the regularjudge is ab-
sent, or can not properlypreside, it shallbe

attend and hold court, was held constitu-
tional. Hughes v . Com ., 89 Ky ., 227 ; 11 R.,
424 .

Murray v.East End Co.,22 R., 1477, and see
(Carroll's)Code ,secs.334-5, and notes thereto.
(9) Specialjudge- generally. Ifthe special
judge whom the partiesselectedacted with-
out being sworn, the objectionwas waived
by the acquiescenceof the partiesat the
time . Salter v . Salter, 6 Bush , 624.
(10) Special judge electedto try such cases
as the regularjudge could not properlytry
at a particularterm , had no power to render
judgment in cases at the succeedingterm,
another attorney having been electedas
specialjudge at that term. Childersv.Little,
96 Ky ., 376 ; 16 R., 521 ; Small v . Reeves , 104
Ky ., 289 ; 20 R., 504.
(11) A specialjudge may hear and decide
caseswhile the regularjudge is holdinghis
court. Paducah Land Co. v . Cochran , 18
R. , 465 .
(12) Itisnot necessarythat a specialjudge
should be a resident of the judicialdistrict
in which he is selected. Breckinridge v.
Com ., 97 Ky ., 267 ; 17 R., 163.
(13) A specialjudge has no power except
such as is necessaryto hold court for the
occasion, thereforea specialjudge had no
authority to act with the other regular
judges in the appointment of an official
indexerforJeffersoncounty. Robertsv.Cain,
97 Ky ., 722 ; 17 R., 459.
(14) Special judge in courts of continuous
session can not serve for more than sixty
days unless by agreement or re-election.
Crane v . Brooke , 22 R., 1271.
(15) When a specialjudge is selectedto
presidein a particularcase,the presumption
is that allordersin the case are made by
him unless the contrary appears from the
record. Bullittv. Eastern Ky . Land Co., 99
Ky ., 324; 18 R., 230.
§ 969. Compensation of specialjudge . Where
the specialjudge electedfor the term is
unable to preside in certain cases and another
specialjudge isselectedto try thesecases,he
is entitledto pay for the days he serves,
although the specialjudge is paid for the
entire term . Norman v . Wood , 98 Ky ., 640 ;

that it should state how the knife was used

(10) Insanity- presumption . Sanity is pre-
sumed by law and the burden of proof of
insanity is on accused. Graham v . Com ., 16

only to the extent of preponderance of
evidence, such as will create a doubt of guilt.

(11) Killing of officer. The killingof one

120; Dilger v . Com ., 88 Ky ., 551 ; 11 R., 67 ;
Arnold v . Com ., 21 R., 1566.
(12) Malice the existenceof, like any
other fact, must be left to the jury . Bush v.
Com ., 78 Ky ., 268.
(13) Reckless shooting. One who , without
lawful excuse, firesa pistolin a room crowded
with people and kills another is guilty of
murder . Brown v . Com ., 13 R. , 372 .
(14 ) Self-defense - defense of another - de-
fense of one'sproperty. Defense of one'sown
person. Rapp v . Com ., 14 В. М. , 494 ; Mere-
dith v . Com ., 18 B. M. , 49 ; Payne v . Com ., 1

act so that the person struck, stabbed, thrust or shot shall die thereof
within six months next thereafter, shallbe confinedin the penitentiary

construed to change the law of malice in respect to any other offense.

Rape , Abduction .

thediscretionof the jury.
§ 1153. Attempttorapeinfantundertwelve. Whoever shallattempt to com-
mit rape upon the body of an infantunder twelve years of age shallbe

untary manslaughter is proper, but not as

§ 1152. (1) Degrees of offense. One indicted

stances " was erroneous ; the last words were

§ 1153.Indictment. Attempted rape upon

And see notes to secs . 1154-58 .

§ 1154-57 ] [Ch . 36 .CRIMES AND PUNISHMENTS .

§ 1154. Carnallyknowingfemaleagainstherconsent. Whoever shall unlawfully
carnally know a female, of and above twelve years of age, against
her willor consent,or by force,or whilstshe isinsensible,shallbe guilty
of rape, and punished by confinement in the penitentiarynot lessthan
ten nor more than twenty years,or by death,in the discretionof the jury.
§ 1155. Carnallyknowingfemaleundertwelve,or an idiot. Whoever shall car-
nally know a female under the age of twelve years, or an idiot, shall
be confined in the penitentiary not less than ten nor more than twenty
years .
§ 1156. Abductionof girlunderfourteen. Whoever ,being above the age of
fourteen years ,shall unlawfully take, without her consent ,any unmarried
girl,under the age of fourteenyears,out of the possessionof her father,
mother , or other person having the lawful custody and charge of her,
against the will and consent of such person, shall be confined in the
penitentiaryfrom one to two years,or finedfrom one to fivehundred dol-
lars,or both, at the discretionof the jury.
§ 1157. Decoyingorenticingaway or harboringchildunderten. Whoever ,being
above the age of fourteen years , shall unlawfully lead or take away , or
decoy,or enticeaway ,or detain any childunder the age of ten years,with
intent to deprive the parent or other person having the lawful care.
charge or possessionof such child,or with intentto stealany articleof
value upon or about the person of such child, or shall, with any such
intention, receive, conceal or harbor such child, knowing itto have been
so taken or enticedaway , shallbe confinedin the penitentiarynot less
than one nor more than three years. But no person claiming in good
faithto be the parent of such child,or to have the rightto itspossession,
shallincur the penalty prescribedin thisor the next precedingsection.
§ 11574. Holdingpersonforransom- jurisdiction. If any person or persons
shall,forciblyor otherwise,hold any person againsttheirwillfor the pur-
pose of unlawfully obtaininga ransom for the releaseof said person or
aid or abet any person thus offending, shall, on convictionthereof, be
deemed guiltyof a felony, and shallbe confinedin the penitentiarynot
lessthan two nor more than twenty-one years. Any person or persons
charged with such offensemay be tried in any county into or through
which the person or child so seized, inveigled, decoyed, kidnapped ,
abducted or otherwise taken shall have been carried or brought . (This
section is an act of March 21 , 1902.)
§ 1154. (1) Aiders and abettors may be in-
dicted as principaloffendersin the second
degree, whether they be women or men .
Kessler v. Com ., 12 Bush , 18.
(2) Degrees of the offense. One charged
with rape is entitledto have the jury in-
structedas to the whole law applicableto
the case, and any of itsdegreesas defined
by sections262-3 of CriminalCode. Bethel
v. Com ., 80 Ky ., 526; 4 R.,487. And where
the evidencejustifiesit, an instructionfor
carnallyknowing the infantfemaleshouldbe
given. Young v. Com ., 96 Ky ., 573; 16 R.,
496 ; and under an indictment for rape the
accused may be convicted of unlawfully de-
taining a woman . Fagan v . Com ., 18 R., 714 ;
Fenston v .Com ., 82 Ky .,549 ; 7 R.,55.
(3 ) Indictment need not use the word
" ravish" if it charges offense in language of
statute. Wilkey v . Com ., 104 Ky ., 325 ; 20
R. , 578 .
(4 ) Offense of rape. To constitute the of-
fense of rape it is not necessary that the act
should be committed against the woman's
will; it is sufficientthat it is committed
without her consent. Malone v . Com ., 91
Ky .,307; 12 R., 895; and seeWhite v. Com .,
96 Ky ., 180 ; 16 R., 421.

§ 1158. Unlawfullytakingor detainingwoman againsther will. Whoever shall

knowledge, shallbe confined in the penitentiarynot lessthan two nor

SUBDIVISION IV .
Robbery , Burglary .
§ 1159. Punishmentforrobberyor burglary,or forhavingburglarioustools. Every
person guiltyof robbery or burglary shallbe confinedin the penitentiary
not lessthan two nor more than ten years. If any person shallhave or
keep in his possessionany tools, implements , or other things used by
burglarsforhouse-breaking,forcingdoors,windows,locks,or buildings,
or other places where goods, wares, or merchandise or money is kept,
with theintentionof usingsaidtoolsor implementsburglariously,shall
be confined in the penitentiary not lessthan two nor more than ten years .
§ 1158. (1) Constituents of offense. It is
sufficient if the act was done without the
consent of the woman ; and if she was un-
conscious, or incapableof exercisingher will,
the act should be regarded as done without
her consent. Malone v . Com ., 91 Ky ., 307 ;
12 R. , 895 ; Couch v . Com ., 16 R., 477.
(2) Degree of offense. The statute creates
a lesseroffensethan that of rape or attempt
to commit rape. Evans v . Com ., 79 Ky ., 414 ;
3 R. , 30 ; Howell v. Com ., 5 R., 174. And
under an indictment for rape the accused
may be convictedof unlawfullydetaininga
woman . Fagan v. Com ., 18 R., 714.
(3) Indictmentchargingaccused with un-
lawfullyand forciblydetaining, is not suffi-
cient the taking or detention against her
willmust be alleged. Wilder v.Com .,81 Ky .,
591 ; 5 R., 635. It is not sufficientthat the
attempt to have carnal knowledge of her
was against her will. Krambeil v. Com .,
8 R., 605. Averment that accused "unlaw-
fully" detaineda certainfemale,for the pur-
pose of carnal knowledge with her, etc., is
sufficient; it need not be alleged that the
accusedacted"feloniously." Higginsv. Com .,
94 Ky ., 54 ; 14 R., 729. A charge of taking
and detainingdoes not charge two offenses;
eitherthe taking or detention, or both, con-
stitute the single offense described by the
statute. Owens v. Com ., 5 R., 174. It is not
necessary to state the manner of the de-
tention. Gargill v . Com ., 12 R., 149.
(4 ) Statements made by prosecutrix soon
after alleged detention are not competent
againstaccused. Douglas v.Com .,24 R.,562.
§ 1159. (1) Burglary - constituents of of-
fense. It is not necessary to prove that
goods, etc., were actually stolen; it is suffi-
cient if the house is feloniously broken and
entered with the intention of doing so. Olive
v . Com ., 5 Bush , 376. But the indictment
shouldspecifythe kind of felonyintendedto
be committed ; it is not sufficientto charge
with "intentto commit a felony." Kyle v.
Com ., 23 R. , 708 .
(2) Degrees of offense larceny res judi-
cata. An acquittalor conviction of burglary
bars a prosecutionforlarcenyformingpart of
the same transaction for which the defend-
ant was tried under the indictment for
burglary. Triplettv.Com .,84 Ky .,193; 8 R.,
67; so as to prosecutionfor robbery. Com .
v. Prewitt , 82 Ky ., 240 ; 6 R., 195.
(3) Housebreaking - under indictment for
burglary accused may be convicted of. Com .
v . Hurd , 22 R. , 509 .
(4 ) Robbery_indictment evidence. Under
an indictmentchargingthat defendantfelon-
iouslytook certaintreasurynotes, the prop-
erty of "M ," in hispresenceand againsthis
will by putting him in fear of some im-
mediate injuryto his person, the Common-
wealth must prove that the treasury notes
were taken in "M's " presenceby puttinghim
in fear. Glass v . Com ., 6 Bush , 436.
(5) Any force sufficientto take property
from personalpossessionof another against
his willconstitutesrobbery, althoughperson
robbed is not in fear. Jones v . Com ., 23 R. ,
2081 ; Com . v . Davis , 23 R., 1717 ; 22 R., 515.
(6) Matter of defense_drunkenness . Ac-

son therein,or to stealproperty,money ,or anything of value therefrom,

§ 1164. Breakingwarehouse, storehouse, officeor room on boat,in nighttime. If
any person shallfeloniously, in the night or day , break any warehouse ,
storehouse,office,shop,or room ,in a steam,wharf ,or other boat,whether
such place be or be not a depositoryforgoods,wares,or merchandise,and
whether the goods , wares and merchandise be or be not exposed for sale
in such place, with intentto steal,or shallfeloniouslytake therefrom or
destroyany goods,wares,or merchandise,or otherthing of value,whether
the owner or other person be or be not in such house , office, room , or shop ,

deprivethe owner of hisproperty, or to con-
vert it to the use of the taker . An indict-

classification.summary: This section of the Kentucky Statutes from 1903 outlines several misdemeanor offenses. These include refusing to obey a summons of an officer, conspiring to aid in a false prosecution, obstructing street railroads, passenger disturbances on streetcars (including refusal to pay fare), operating portable engines on highways, dog-fighting and chicken-fighting, and forging petitions. Penalties range from fines to imprisonment.
classification.reasoning: The provided statute text details various misdemeanor offenses and their corresponding penalties. None of the described offenses or their punishments contain any explicit or implicit racial distinctions. The statute focuses on general public order, safety, and legal processes, applicable to all individuals regardless of race. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law.

classification.summary: This statute clarifies how advancements made to heirs affect the distributable share of a widow in an estate. It states that advancements to distributees do not reduce the widow's personal estate share. The statute further details how advancements are to be accounted for in cases of partial intestacy, the right to dispute their correctness, satisfaction of debt, estimation of value, and what is regarded as an advancement, including gifts to grandchildren and conveyances to a daughter's husband.

There is no mention of race, nor any provisions that implicitly or explicitly discriminate based on race. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law. It lists various items such as manufactured cloth, carpeting, furniture, books, saddles, bridles, chairs, cradles, poultry, sheep, wearing apparel, provisions, provender for livestock, washing apparatus, sewing machines, family portraits, cooking stoves, and utensils. § 1702. (1) Abandonment . Where a debtor
removes from his residence with the inten-
tion of permanently locatingelsewhere, his
right to the homestead ceases, although he
may own and cultivateit and have a tenant
thereon ; and the right is not re-established
by his intentionto return, but only relates
to the time when he actuallymakes it his
residence. Carter v . Goodman , 11 Bush , 228.
(2) A debtor having made a contract for
the saleof his homestead, removed from it;
after his removal the purchaser abandoned
the contract, and the debtor was prevented
by his death from returning; after his death
the widow returned , and was entitled to a
homestead . Persifullv . Hind , 88 Ky ., 296 ;
10 R. , 880 .
(3) A debtor sold his homestead and in-
vested proceedsin a homestead in another
State,where he residedseveralyears; having
sold this homestead and invested proceeds
in another homestead in this State, it is
subject to his debts createdbefore he re-
moved from State. Caldwell v . Seivers, 85
Ky ., 38 ; 8 R., 636 ; and see Burch v . Atchin-
son,82 Ky .,585 ; 6 R., 636 ; Wickliffev .Zeller,

ticular case. See Campbell v . Potter, 16 R.,
535 ; Central Asylum v . Craven , 98 Ky ., 105;

736; 23 R.,2187; Herring v.Johnston,24 R.,
1940; 24 R., 1737; 24 R., 2503.
(5) Bought with exempt wages . Homestead
paid for by wages exempt from debts can
not be subjected to the payment of a debt
created beforeitspurchase . Wallace v.Mason ,
100 Ky ., 560 ; 18 R. , 935 .
(6) Commonwealth exemption against. As
a general rule, the homestead can not be
claimed against debts due the State, but the
husband is entitledto a homestead as against
a debt due an asylum for keeping his wife.
Central Asylum v . Craven , 98 Ky ., 105 ; 17 R. ,
667; and see Com . v . Cook , 8 Bush ,220 ; Com .
v . Lay , 12 Bush , 283 ; and see Holburn v .
Pfaumiller, 24 R., 1613; Riddle v . Fannin ,
24 R. , 1737 .
(7) Descent . Debtor is entitled to home-
stead in property derived by descent, and
upon which he resides, as against debts
created prior to time he received it. Meador
v . Meador , 88 Ky ., 217 ; 10 R., 783 ; Jewell v .
Clark, 78 Ky .,398; 106 Ky .,274; 20 R.,1822;
11 R. , 391. But where the debtor has never

906 .
(8) Devise of homestead . Owner of home-
stead may disposeof it by will, and unless

classification.summary: This statute outlines the process for valuing and allotting a homestead exemption for debtors facing execution, attachment, or judgment. It specifies that a portion of land occupied as a homestead, not exceeding one thousand dollars in value, can be selected by the defendant and set apart by appraisers. The exemption continues after the debtor's death for the benefit of their widow and children, but is estimated in allotting dower. The statute also details requirements for waiving such exemptions.

classification.title: FIRE ESCAPES
classification.summary: This act, passed on February 13, 1888, mandates that all buildings in cities with over ten thousand inhabitants, that are three or more stories high (excluding private residences and certain stores/warehouses), must be equipped with metallic fire escapes. The chief of the fire department is responsible for determining the number, kind, construction, and location of these fire escapes. The owner, agent, lessee, or occupant is notified and given thirty days to comply. If the owner fails to act, the tenant may have the work done at their own expense, with a lien on the property. Penalties are outlined for violations.

It outlines the responsibilities of building owners, tenants, and fire departments in ensuring fire safety. There is no mention of race, nor any provisions that implicitly or explicitly discriminate based on race. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law.

It also permits additional levies for specific debt obligations incurred before September 28, 1891.

classification.title: Kentucky Statutes 1903, Chapter 52, Section 1840: Fiscal Courts - Jurisdiction and Powers
classification.summary: This statute outlines the general jurisdiction and powers of fiscal courts in Kentucky. It details their authority to appropriate county funds, erect and maintain public buildings (including jails), bridges, and highways, manage county fiscal affairs and property, provide for the poor and sick poor (including establishing a poorhouse, farm, or hospital), and levy taxes as authorized by law. It also includes case law annotations regarding county liability for injuries due to negligence in maintaining public infrastructure and actions brought by or against counties.

It covers the maintenance of public infrastructure, provision for the poor and sick, and fiscal management. There is no mention of race, segregation, or any discriminatory practices. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law. The document type is 'codes' as it appears to be part of a compiled statute collection from 1903.

classification.title: Bonds to Fund Indebtedness
classification.summary: This statute authorizes Kentucky counties, through their fiscal courts, to issue new bonds to replace outstanding bonds issued prior to September 28, 1891, for railroad purposes or otherwise. The new bonds cannot exceed the amount of old bonds and outstanding interest, and have specific terms regarding denomination, maturity (up to 40 years), interest rate (up to 6% semi-annually), and payment location. The fiscal court can sell these new bonds at not less than par or exchange them for old bonds. The proceeds or exchanged bonds must be used solely for liquidating old outstanding bonds, interest, and associated costs. The county court clerk is required to maintain a detailed record of all bond transactions, which is open to taxpayer inspection. A specific condition is mentioned for calling in bonds issued on account of donations or subscriptions to railroad company capital stock before issuing new bonds for exchange or sale.

It outlines the process for counties to manage their outstanding financial obligations, particularly those related to railroad funding. classification.summary: This statute addresses fraudulent and preferential conveyances of property. It states that a voluntary conveyance made without valuable consideration is void as to existing liabilities but not necessarily as to subsequent creditors or purchasers without notice. It also outlines conditions under which conveyances can be deemed constructively fraudulent, such as contracts for board and support of the grantor, conveyances where consideration is paid by another, and gifts from a father to his child to the detriment of creditors. The statute also touches upon insurance for a wife's benefit, limitations for setting aside conveyances, voluntary conveyances on the eve of marriage, and the intent of the grantor.

classification.title: Conveyances in Contemplation of Insolvency
classification.summary: This statute addresses fraudulent and preferential conveyances made by debtors in contemplation of insolvency. It states that such sales, mortgages, assignments, judgments suffered, or other devices designed to prefer one or more creditors over others will operate as an assignment and transfer of all the debtor's property for the benefit of all creditors proportionally. However, it includes an exception for mortgages made in good faith to secure a simultaneously created debt, provided they are recorded within thirty days of execution. The statute also includes provisions regarding the recording of written evidence of loans or reservations of property, and the effect of possession without proper recording.

classification.title: Game and Birds Protection Statutes
classification.summary: These statutes, enacted in 1903, establish regulations for the protection of various birds and game animals. They prohibit the catching, killing, or possession of doves during specific months, and song or insectivorous birds at any time unless they are destructive to crops. Quail, partridge, and pheasant are protected at all times. Destroying nests or eggs of wild birds, except predatory ones, is also forbidden. Penalties for violations include fines, with a portion going to the informer. Possession of protected animals or birds during prohibited times is considered prima facie evidence of unlawful activity. Selling protected species during prohibited times carries the same penalty as unlawful taking. Each offense is distinct and punishable separately. Magistrates are empowered to issue warrants for arrests and require bail for individuals violating these provisions.
classification.reasoning: The provided statute text details regulations concerning the protection of game and birds in Kentucky. It outlines prohibited times for catching or killing certain species, restrictions on the destruction of nests and eggs, and associated penalties. There is no mention of race, nor are there any provisions that implicitly or explicitly discriminate based on race. The focus is solely on wildlife conservation and the enforcement of hunting and possession laws. Therefore, this statute is not a Jim Crow law. The document type is classified as 'criminal_laws' because it defines offenses and penalties. The confidence is high as the content is clearly unrelated to racial segregation or discrimination.

classification.title: An Act for the Protection of Game and Birds
classification.summary: This statute outlines regulations for the protection of game birds and other wild birds within the State of Kentucky. It prohibits the killing, possession, purchase, sale, transport, or shipment of wild birds other than game birds, as well as their plumage, skin, or body parts. It also prohibits the destruction of nests or eggs of non-game birds. The statute defines what constitutes a game bird and specifies penalties for violations, including fines and imprisonment. Exemptions are provided for individuals holding certificates for scientific purposes. Enforcement duties are assigned to mayors, market-masters, and police forces, with penalties for officers failing to perform their duties.

classification.title: GUARDIANS, BOARD OF FOR CHILDREN IN CERTAIN COUNTIES
classification.summary: This statute establishes a board responsible for the care and supervision of neglected and dependent children under sixteen years of age in certain counties. The board has the power to take children into its care if they are abandoned, neglected, cruelly treated, begging, have habitually drunken or unfit parents, are kept in vicious associations, are known to be vicious or incorrigible, or have parents living in unlawful cohabitation. The board is to provide temporary homes, ensure moral training, and can commit children to orphan asylums, industrial schools, or the State reformatory, or have them indentured as apprentices or adopted. The statute details the process for petitioning the court and issuing writs for child custody.
classification.reasoning: The statute concerns the welfare and care of children, specifically addressing issues of neglect, abandonment, and dependency. It outlines the powers and duties of a board established to oversee these children and provides mechanisms for their placement and care. There is no mention of race, nor are there any provisions that implicitly suggest racial discrimination. The statute appears to be a general child welfare law. The document type is inferred as 'codes' because it is presented as a section within a compiled statute book (Kentucky Statutes 1903).

classification.title: Husband and Wife: Property Rights
classification.summary: This statute, enacted in 1894 and codified in 1903, defines the property rights of husbands and wives. It states that a husband has no estate or interest in his wife's property, real or personal, owned at the time of or acquired after marriage. The wife holds all her estate to her separate and exclusive use, free from her husband's debts, liabilities, or control. Her estate is liable for her debts contracted before marriage and for those contracted after marriage, except as provided in the act. The statute also includes notes on the effect of the act on marriages contracted before its passage, the right of a wife to recover land sold by her husband without her joining in the conveyance, the extinguishment of debts due from a wife to her husband by marriage, and the participation of a married woman in fraud.
classification.reasoning: The statute explicitly deals with the property rights of married individuals within the context of marriage and divorce. It focuses on the legal and financial separation of spousal property. There is no mention of race, nor are there any provisions that implicitly discriminate based on race. The statute's focus is solely on marital property law. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law. The document type is 'codes' as it is presented as part of a compiled statute collection (Kentucky Statutes 1903).

classification.title: Husband and Wife - Property Rights
classification.summary: This statute outlines the property rights of married women in Kentucky as of 1903. It grants married women the ability to acquire, hold, sell, and dispose of personal property independently, and to make contracts and sue or be sued as if unmarried. However, it restricts her ability to make executory contracts for real estate (selling, conveying, or mortgaging) unless her husband joins. She retains the right to rent out her real estate and collect rents. The statute also addresses the validity of personal property transfers between spouses, requiring them to be in writing, acknowledged, and recorded to be valid against third parties, and notes that such transfers are void if fraudulent. It also references previous statutes and case law regarding separate estates and the wife's ability to mortgage her property to secure her husband's debts.
classification.reasoning: The statute deals with the property rights of married women and does not contain any explicit or implicit racial distinctions. It focuses on the legal and financial autonomy of women within marriage. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law. The confidence is high because the text clearly defines the scope of the statute, which is limited to marital property rights and does not involve race. The document type is 'codes' as it appears to be part of a compiled set of statutes (Kentucky Statutes 1903).

classification.title: Impeachment
classification.summary: This section outlines the process for impeaching public officers in Kentucky. It details the petition process to the House of Representatives, the role of committees, summoning witnesses, and the procedures for the Senate to hear the impeachment. It also specifies how legal documents and summons should be served, including leaving a copy with a 'white member of his family over the age of sixteen years' if personal service is not possible.
classification.reasoning: The statute itself is about the impeachment process, which is not inherently a Jim Crow law. However, section 2172, subsection 3, contains a racial indicator: 'The precept shall be served in person, or a copy left at his residence with some white member of his family over the age of sixteen years, together with a copy of the impeachment.' This specific phrasing implies a racial distinction in how legal documents are served, suggesting that only a 'white member' of the family would suffice for service if the accused was not personally present. This is a subtle but significant indicator of racial bias in legal procedures, which is characteristic of the Jim Crow era. While the core subject matter is impeachment, this detail warrants a closer look and flags it for human review to determine if this procedural detail was part of a broader pattern of racial discrimination in legal enforcement. Given the explicit mention of 'white member', the racial indicator is 'implicit' as it doesn't name a specific race being discriminated against, but rather implies a racial preference in service. The confidence is high that it's not a direct Jim Crow law, but the racial indicator makes it ambiguous enough to require human review.

classification.summary: This statute outlines the conditions under which investment companies organized in other states can conduct business in Kentucky. It requires them to file their charter, establish a local office and agents, and make deposits with the State Treasurer. The statute also includes a retaliatory clause: if other states impose greater taxes, penalties, or requirements on Kentucky investment companies, Kentucky will impose the same on companies from those states. It also addresses situations where out-of-state deposits are less than required by Kentucky law.

classification.title: JAILERS. Duties and Powers.
classification.summary: This statute outlines the duties and powers of jailers in Kentucky. It details the county court's role in prescribing rules for jail governance, cleanliness, and prisoner treatment, with the power to enforce these rules and punish jailers for disobedience or neglect. It also specifies that jailers can execute process from any court, are governed by laws applicable to sheriffs, and must keep jails clean, warm, and provide adequate bedding. The statute also allows for the appointment of deputies and, in Jefferson County, the election of a physician for the jail. Case law is included regarding indictments for jailer misconduct.
classification.reasoning: The statute focuses on the administrative and operational aspects of jails and the duties of jailers. It does not contain any provisions that explicitly or implicitly discriminate based on race. The rules and responsibilities outlined apply to all individuals confined in the jail, regardless of their race. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law. The category is 'incarceration' as it directly pertains to the management of jails and prisoners.

classification.title: General Provisions Regarding Liens, Lis Pendens, Attachments, and Executions
classification.summary: This statute outlines the procedural requirements for filing notices of legal actions affecting real estate (liens, title disputes, possession, use, taxes, assessments, charges) and notices of attachments or executions. It mandates that such actions or proceedings, or orders/judgments/sales stemming from them, will not affect subsequent purchasers, lessees, or encumbrancers for value without notice, unless a memorandum detailing the action, parties involved, and affected real estate is filed with the county clerk. The clerk is responsible for recording, indexing, and maintaining these notices. The statute also specifies requirements for notices of attachments and executions, including details of the issuing court, parties, and dates. It emphasizes that a levy of execution is only effective against a purchaser without notice if the record is made as provided.
classification.reasoning: The statute concerns procedural requirements for filing legal notices related to real estate transactions and legal proceedings. It establishes rules for how these notices must be filed with the county clerk to be effective against subsequent purchasers, lessees, or encumbrancers. There is no mention of race, nor any indication of differential treatment based on race. The statute appears to be a general civil procedure law related to property rights and legal filings. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law.

It establishes the priority of these liens over other debts of the owner and subsequently created liens.

classification.title: Liens. Railroads and Other Improvements.
classification.summary: This section of the Kentucky Statutes from 1903 outlines liens related to railroads and other improvements. It details liability for damages caused by steamboats and other vessels, the enforcement of liens through attachment, bond requirements for attachments, the release of attached property through bond, and the ability of lien-holders to unite as plaintiffs. It also states that liens are not enforceable against a purchaser without notice unless suit is instituted within one year or notice is indorsed on the vessel's enrollment. Article III specifically addresses liens of employees and materialmen on property assigned for the benefit of creditors, including mines, railroads, turnpikes, and canal companies.

It also specifies how the lien attaches and can be enforced when a business is suspended, sold, transferred, or its property is levied upon.

classification.title: Limitation of Actions - Actions for Recovery of Real Estate
classification.summary: This statute outlines the conditions under which the statute of limitations for actions to recover real property can be extended. It specifies that if a person is an infant, married woman, or of unsound mind at the time their right to sue accrues, they have three years after the disability is removed to bring the action, even if the standard fifteen-year period has expired. It also includes various case law interpretations regarding adverse possession, easements, remaindermen, trust estates, vendor's rights, and widow's dower rights.
classification.reasoning: The statute deals with the legal concept of the statute of limitations for recovering real property and the conditions that can toll (pause) this limitation period, such as minority, marriage, or mental incapacity. There is no mention of race, nor are there any provisions that implicitly or explicitly discriminate based on race. The statute applies universally to all individuals regardless of their race. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law.

(25) Commencement of action. The action

(26) Corporation_stockholder . If a cor-
poration can rely upon lapse of time against
a stockholder who demands the evidence of
titleto his stock, the statute will not begin
to run until the stockholder is notified that
his titleis disputed. Limitation runs against
a stockholder as to dividends on his stock
which have been appropriated by the cor-
poration. Mercer County Court v . S. M. &
H. T. R. Co., 10 Bush , 254.
(27) Damages for violation of contract in
restraint of trade is barred after lapse of
five years from date of contract. Davis v .
Brown , 98 Ky ., 475 ; 17 R., 1428.
(28) Decedent'sestates. A promiseby one
of two personal representatives takes the
case out of the statute as to both . Hord v .
Lee , 4 Mon. , 36 ; Northcut v . Wilkinson , 12
B. M. ,408. See Head v . Manners , 5 J. J. М. ,
255. Debt barred by statute may be paid
by the personalrepresentative; but the heir
or deviseemay , by proper proceedings, re-
quire the personal representativeto plead
the statute. Payne v. Pusey, 8 Bush , 564.
The heir'sliabilityfor his ancestor'sdebt is
not within the meaning of the statute"a
liabilitycreatedby statute." TrusteesKy .
F. O. S. v. Fleming, 10 Bush, 234. Where
the right of action vests in the personal
representative, the disabilityof the heir
will not prevent the running of the statute.
Darnall v . Adams , 13 B. M. , 273 ; Couch v .
Couch, 9 B. M., 160; and if the representa-
tivepermits a bar to take place, the heiris
bound by his laches. Rosson v. Anderson,
9 В. М. ,423 .
(29) Fraud or mistake. If the party isap-
prised of the fraud or mistake at the time
it is perpetrated, he must sue within five
years; but if he is not then apprisedof it,
he must sue within fiveyears after the dis-
covery , but in no case can he sue after ten
years. Brown v. Brown , 91 Ky ., 639; 12 R.,
280 ; see further notes to sec.2519, and Webb
v .Webb , 23 R., 2515 .
(30) Ignoranceof statuteof limitationcan
not be pleaded as a defense. Hopperton v .
L. & N. R. R.,17 R., 1322.
(31) Malpractice actionagainstphysician
is barred in five- not one- years. Menifee
v . Alexander , 21 R. , 980.
(32) Merchants . Merchant tailors are
deemed merchants within the meaning of
the statute. Hearn v . Van Ingen , 7 Bush ,
426 .
(33) Mistake of law or fact. A payment
of a debt barred by the statute of limitations
can not be recovered back on a plea of mis-
take of law or fact. Hubbard v . City of
Hickman , 4 Bush , 204.
(34) New promise or acknowledgment .
An express promise to pay , or an express ac-
knowledgment of the debt as a debt due at
the time , coupled with the original consid-
eration, must have been made within the
time limited by the statute for bringing
the action. Gray v. Lawridge, 2 Bibb, 284;
French v. Frazier, 7 J. J. M., 425. But if
the acknowledgment is accompanied by any
circumstances or expressions which repel the
idea of an intention or willingness to pay ,
the debt is not thereby revived. Warren v.
Perry , 5 Bush , 447 ; Gray v . McDowell , 6
Bush , 475. Defendant's statement that he
had once owed plaintiff, but supposed his
brotherhad paid it in Virginia (where the
original transaction took place); and if his
brotherhad not paid it,he owed it yet, was
not sufficient. Bell v . Rowland , Hard ., 301.
So of an admission that certain work had
been done and ought to be paid for. Head v .
Manners , 5 J. J. M., 255. Creating a trust
upon personalestate, by will, for the pay-
ment of debts will not revive a debt which
is barred. Campbell v. Sullivan, Hard ., 17.
Acknowledgment that an account is allright
is too indefinite. Harrison v. Handley, 1
Bibb , 443 ; but see Ditto v . Ditto, 4 Dana ,
502. Statement made by defendant , when
the account was presentedto him, that it
was just so far as he knew ; that he leftit
to the other party and had kept no account
himself, but that plaintiffwas indebted to
him , is not sufficient. Tillet v . Linsey , 6 J.
J. M. , 337. Agreement of a debtor that a
settlement made by the creditor and a third
person should be examined by eitherparty
will not take the case out of the statute .
Ormsby v.Letcher,3 Bibb,269. The acknowl-
edgment to take the case out of the statute
must be made to the creditor, or some one
actingforhim,not to a stranger. Trousdale
v. Anderson, 9 Bush , 276; Hargis v. Sewell,
87 Ky ., 63; 9 R., 920. New promise by
executor will not revive the right against
the devisee. Grotenkemper v. Bryson, 79
Ky ., 353; 2 R., 335. Promise by one per-
sonal representativetakes the case out of
the statute as to all. Hord v . Lee , 4 Mon. ,
36; Northcut v . Wilkerson , 12 B. M. , 408 .(35) An admission that the account is just,
is enough, for it can not be just if it has
been paid. Ditto v. Ditto, 4 Dana , 502.

classification.title: Medicine and Surgery - Registration of Physicians
classification.summary: This statute outlines the requirements for practicing medicine in Kentucky. It mandates that physicians must register with the county clerk, providing their authority to practice, age, address, place of birth, and medical school affiliation. This registration must be accompanied by an oath. The owner , agent or lesseeof every coal mine , whether slope, shaft or

driven more than sixty feet in advance of a break -through or air-way ;
and all break-throughs or air-ways , except those last made near the
working-face of the mine , shall be closed up and made air-tight by
brattice,trap-doors or otherwise,so that the currentsof airin circulation
in the mine may sweep to the interiorof the excavationswhere the per-
sons employed in the mines are at work ; and allmines governed by this
statute shall be provided with artificialmeans of producing ventilation,
such as suction or forcing fans, exhaust steam , furnaces , or other con-
trivances, of such capacity and power as to produce and maintain an
abundant supply of air. All mines generating fire-damp shall be kept

examined every morning with a safety lamp , by a competent person or

classification.title: Annexation or Reduction of Territory for Municipal Corporations
classification.summary: This statute outlines the process by which a city's general council can annex new territory or reduce its existing boundaries. It requires an ordinance defining the territory, publication of the ordinance, and a waiting period. Residents or freeholders of the affected territory can file a petition in circuit court to remonstrate against the annexation or reduction. The court will then determine if the annexation/reduction is in the city's interest and will not cause manifest injury, considering the percentage of freeholders who have remonstrated. If 75% or more have remonstrated, annexation/reduction will only proceed if it is shown to materially retard the prosperity of the city and its inhabitants.
classification.reasoning: The statute details the legal procedures for changing the geographical boundaries of a city. It outlines the steps for annexation and reduction of territory, including the role of the general council, publication requirements, and the right of residents to petition the circuit court to object. The criteria for approving or rejecting such changes are based on the city's interest and the potential injury to property owners, with a specific threshold for freeholder remonstrance. There is no mention of race or any provisions that would inherently discriminate based on race. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law. The document type is 'codes' as it appears to be part of a compiled set of statutes (Kentucky Statutes 1903).

It also mandates annual examination and inspection of the police force.
classification.reasoning: The provided statute text details the operational aspects of municipal police and fire departments, including the appointment, qualifications, and duties of police officers, as well as the handling of evidence. There is no mention of race, nor are there any provisions that implicitly suggest racial segregation or discrimination. The qualifications listed (citizenship, residency, sobriety, integrity, law-abiding behavior, no felony conviction) are general and not tied to race. Therefore, this statute is not a Jim Crow law.

classification.title: Kentucky Statutes 1903, Section 2896-964 and 2896.4
classification.summary: This statute outlines regulations for first-class police and fire departments in Kentucky cities. It details the powers of the board of public safety regarding officer inspection, removal for inefficiency, and disciplinary procedures for fire department members. It also specifies exemptions for police officers from military or jury duty and civil process while on duty, and prohibits them from belonging to political organizations. The text includes an amendment to an act for the government of cities of the first class, approved in 1893, and references a repealed act from 1900 that was deemed unconstitutional.
classification.reasoning: The provided statute text focuses on the organization, discipline, and operational aspects of municipal police and fire departments in Kentucky cities of the first class. It details procedures for examining, hearing, and determining charges against members, as well as exemptions from certain civic duties for police officers. There is no mention of race, nor are there any provisions that implicitly or explicitly discriminate based on race. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law. The document type is classified as 'codes' as it appears to be part of a compiled statute collection from 1903.

classification.summary: This statute outlines the establishment and management of a firemen's pension fund in cities of the first class. It details how the fund is financed through taxes, withheld pay for disciplinary infractions, fines, rewards, and assessments on fire department members. The board of public safety is designated as the trustee, responsible for investing the fund and deciding on pension applications for disabled members, their widows, dependent children, or parents. The fund's principal and interest are to be used for pension payments.

If the territory to be annexed is not already an incorporated city, town, or village, the annexation must be approved by a four-sevenths majority vote of the qualified voters in that territory after public notice. The statute also details procedures for redistricting or changing ward boundaries based on population changes and the publication requirements for ordinances related to these changes.
classification.reasoning: The statute deals with the administrative and procedural aspects of municipal governance, specifically the expansion of city boundaries and the redrawing of wards. It does not contain any language that explicitly or implicitly discriminates based on race. The requirements for annexation and redistricting are based on population density, municipal need, and voter approval, not on racial considerations. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law.

classification.title: Free Public Library Provisions for Cities of the Second Class
classification.summary: This statute outlines the establishment, maintenance, and funding of free public libraries in cities of the second class. It details requirements for library boards, their powers, library hours (open until at least 9 PM, closed on Sundays if deemed proper), and funding mechanisms. Funding is derived from 3% of net school taxes and half of net police court fines and costs. It also specifies that libraries must be strictly non-sectarian. A specific section addresses the city of Covington and its accumulated library funds. It also states that no appropriation is required if a city already has a free public library supported by the city.
classification.reasoning: The statute discusses the establishment and funding of free public libraries in cities of the second class. There is no mention of race, segregation, or any differential treatment based on race. The provisions are general and apply to all citizens. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law. The document type is 'codes' as it appears to be part of a compiled set of statutes (indicated by chapter and section numbers like 'Ch. 89' and '§ 32104-105').

It details their control over public ways, places, and property, including construction, maintenance, and improvements. The board is responsible for preparing annual expenditure estimates, managing public buildings, and overseeing departments like the fire department, workhouse, hospital, almshouse, and city prison. It details their powers regarding public infrastructure, finances, and personnel. classification.title: Municipal Corporations - Classification and Boundaries
classification.summary: This statute outlines the process for municipal corporations (towns and cities) in Kentucky to be classified into different classes based on population. It details the procedures for enacting ordinances, filing petitions in circuit court, and publishing notices to change a town's classification. The statute also addresses the maintenance and modification of town boundaries, including annexation and reduction, through ordinances and publication. It clarifies that transfers between classes do not affect existing ordinances or the rights and obligations of the town or its constituents, unless the ordinances conflict with the general laws of the new class. The statute also notes that a court ruling found the part of a similar statute assigning or transferring towns between classes unconstitutional, but the part concerning census-taking is valid.
classification.reasoning: The statute deals with the administrative and legal procedures for classifying municipal corporations based on population and managing their boundaries. There is no mention of race, nor are there any provisions that implicitly suggest racial segregation or discrimination. The statute's focus is purely on the governance and structural organization of towns and cities. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law.

classification.title: PATROLS
classification.summary: This statute outlines the establishment and duties of patrols in Kentucky counties. County courts are authorized to divide counties into districts and appoint patrols consisting of a captain and up to three men. These patrols are to serve for twelve months, unless removed for cause. They must be discreet and sober men, taking an oath to perform their duties faithfully and impartially. Patrols have jurisdiction throughout the county and are tasked with visiting suspected places and places of unlawful assembly. Their compensation is set at a maximum of one dollar for every ten hours of duty, paid from the county levy upon presentation of claims verified by oath.
classification.reasoning: The statute describes the appointment, duties, and compensation of county patrols. There is no mention of race or any provisions that would suggest a racial discriminatory purpose. The focus is on maintaining public peace and order through patrols that have jurisdiction across the entire county. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law.

Additionally, it grants adjacent landowners the right to enter and properly close a well if the owner fails to comply with the waste prevention provisions.

classification.summary: This statute imposes an annual tax of $2,500 on foreign railroad companies that own or operate railroads in Kentucky and have terminal facilities, regardless of whether they conduct interstate commerce. Additionally, it defines a 'tax-broker' as someone who purchases lands sold for taxes aggregating $500 or more, requiring them to obtain a license and pay a fee of 15% of their purchases. The statute also details an organization tax for domestic corporations, which is one-tenth of one percent of their authorized capital stock, due upon incorporation and any subsequent increase. No corporate powers can be exercised until this tax is paid.
