classification.summary: This section of the Kentucky Statutes from 1903 outlines the appointment, duties, and responsibilities of Revenue Agents. It details their oath, bond requirements, and their duty to identify and list omitted property for taxation, as well as collect due license taxes. It also specifies procedures for reporting to the court and the Auditor of Public Accounts, and the consequences for non-compliance.
classification.reasoning: The provided statute text details the administrative and financial functions of revenue agents in Kentucky. It focuses on the process of tax assessment and collection, including identifying omitted property and ensuring license taxes are paid. There is no mention of race, nor are there any provisions that implicitly or explicitly discriminate based on race. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law. The document type is classified as 'codes' as it appears to be part of a compiled set of statutes.

classification.title: Revenue Agent Duties and Compensation
classification.summary: This statute outlines the duties and compensation of a Revenue Agent in Kentucky. The agent is responsible for identifying and pursuing omitted property assessments, prosecuting violators of license laws, investigating the accounts of officers collecting state or county funds, and instituting legal actions to recover money owed to the Commonwealth. The agent is entitled to a commission of twenty percent on recovered taxes and penalties as compensation for their services.

It does not contain any language or provisions that explicitly or implicitly discriminate based on race, nor does it relate to the typical categories of Jim Crow laws such as segregation, voting rights, or marriage restrictions. The document type is inferred as 'codes' because it appears to be part of a compiled body of statutes (Kentucky Statutes 1903).

The text details the process for revenue agents to report collections to the Auditor and the Commonwealth's non-liability for costs and fees, except from collected penalties. It also specifies the Auditor's duty to collect back taxes and fees, including from insurance companies, and the process for investigating delinquent companies.

There is no mention of race, nor are there any provisions that implicitly suggest racial discrimination. The statute focuses on financial and administrative matters related to state revenue. Therefore, it is classified as not a Jim Crow law.

It specifies requirements for moral character, educational ability, age (24 years old), citizenship, and residency. It also details the examination and certification process, including the role of the State Board of Examiners and local county boards, and mentions an exception for counties with cities of the first class.
classification.reasoning: The statute focuses on the administrative and qualification requirements for the position of County Superintendent. It details educational, age, citizenship, and residency requirements, as well as the examination and certification process. There is no mention of race, nor are there any provisions that implicitly suggest racial segregation or discrimination. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law. The document type is inferred as 'codes' because it appears to be part of a compiled set of statutes from 1903, indicated by the chapter and section numbering and the overall structure.

classification.title: Kentucky Statutes 1903, § 4400-1
classification.summary: This statute outlines the qualifications and election process for county superintendents in Kentucky. It includes a provision stating that in counties with a first-class city maintaining a separate school system, no person shall be eligible for county superintendent other than a resident of the county outside of such city or town. This implies a potential for segregation in educational leadership based on residency within or outside of a city with a separate school system, which could have racial implications given the context of Jim Crow era segregation.
classification.reasoning: The statute itself does not explicitly mention race. However, the clause 'In counties embracing any city of the first class, maintaining a system of public schools separate and distinct from the common schools of the county, no person shall be eligible to the office of county superintendent other than a resident of such county, outside of such city or town' is highly suggestive of racial segregation. During the Jim Crow era, separate school systems were often established along racial lines, particularly in larger cities. This provision could have been used to exclude Black individuals from leadership positions in education by restricting eligibility to residents outside of these racially segregated urban school districts. Therefore, it is classified as 'yes' for Jim Crow, with implicit racial indication and a confidence of 0.7, necessitating human review due to the indirect nature of the racial restriction.

classification.title: SCHOOLS - COMMON. County Superintendent.
classification.summary: This statute outlines the duties and responsibilities of a county superintendent of common schools in Kentucky. It details the process for their election, the requirement for an official bond, and their powers regarding school districts, schoolhouses, and furniture. It also specifies that in counties with separate school systems for cities of the first or second class, the county superintendent must reside outside such cities and be elected by voters residing outside those cities.
classification.reasoning: The statute discusses the administrative aspects of common schools, including the role of the county superintendent, the establishment and management of school districts, and the condition of school facilities. While it mentions separate school systems in cities of the first or second class, this separation is based on the existence of distinct public school systems within those cities, not explicitly on race. There is no mention of race or any discriminatory provisions targeting a specific racial group. Therefore, it is classified as not a Jim Crow law.

classification.title: County Superintendent Duties and Census Reporting
classification.summary: This statute outlines the duties of a county superintendent in overseeing common schools, including conducting official visits to schools, advising teachers and trustees, and ensuring proper record-keeping. It also details the superintendent's responsibility for preparing and submitting an annual census report of school-aged children to the Superintendent of Public Instruction, and for any errors made in this report. The statute also covers the notification of changes in district boundaries to trustees and instructions for taking the census.
classification.reasoning: The statute describes the administrative and reporting duties of a county superintendent related to common schools. It focuses on the operational aspects of the school system, such as school visits, teacher and trustee oversight, and census data collection. There is no mention of race, segregation, or any differential treatment based on race. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law. The document type is 'codes' as it appears to be part of a compiled set of statutes (Kentucky Statutes 1903).

classification.summary: This statute outlines the duties of county superintendents and school trustees in Kentucky regarding the reporting of school census data, the supply of textbooks for indigent children, and the payment of teachers. It details procedures for taking census if reports are delinquent, the process for county judges to purchase textbooks for needy students, and the schedule and conditions for teacher salary payments. It also specifies that teachers must have valid certificates to be paid from the common school fund.

classification.summary: This statute outlines penalties for county superintendents who knowingly falsify reports regarding the number of common schools or students. It also details the process for county superintendents to settle their accounts annually with the county judge, including refunding any unexpended funds to the State Treasurer and notifying the Superintendent of Public Instruction. The statute specifies that any recovered funds from a superintendent's malfeasance will be paid into the school fund.
classification.reasoning: The statute focuses on the administrative and financial accountability of county superintendents within the common school system. It details penalties for reporting inaccuracies and procedures for financial settlements. There is no mention of race, segregation, or any differential treatment based on race. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law. The document type is inferred as 'codes' because it appears to be part of a compiled set of statutes (Kentucky Statutes 1903).

Furthermore, it grants the superintendent the power to suspend or remove teachers and trustees for incompetency, neglect of duty, immoral conduct, or other disqualifications, provided proper notice and an opportunity to be heard are given. The superintendent is also designated as the decider of administrative questions concerning common schools, with provisions for appeals.

classification.title: SCHOOLS - COMMON. District Taxation.
classification.summary: This statute outlines the process for local school districts in Kentucky to vote on and implement property taxes for school purposes. It details the requirements for calling an election, who is qualified to vote (including widows and spinsters who are taxpayers or have children of school age), the notice period, and how taxes are levied when district lines divide properties. It also specifies how the tax revenue can be expended and allows for taxes to be voted for up to three years.
classification.reasoning: The statute concerns the mechanism for local school districts to levy taxes for educational purposes. It specifies voter qualifications and election procedures. There is no mention of race, nor are there any provisions that implicitly suggest racial segregation or discrimination. The text focuses solely on the administrative and financial aspects of common schools. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law.

classification.title: Graded Common Schools
classification.summary: This statute outlines the process for establishing and modifying graded common school districts. It specifies that only 'legal white voters' can vote on tax propositions for these schools and that the proposition must be approved by a majority of 'white voters or corporations'. The statute also mentions that the location of the schoolhouse must be within two and a half miles of any point in the district and requires approval from the county superintendent and a majority of the Board of Education for boundary changes. The text explicitly refers to 'legal white voters' and 'white male inhabitants' when discussing voting rights for school taxes and mentions 'corporations' in the context of property assessment for taxation, which could implicitly include entities that were historically segregated.
classification.reasoning: The statute explicitly mentions 'legal white voters' and 'white male inhabitants' in the context of voting on tax propositions for graded common schools. This direct racial qualification for participation in the establishment and funding of public education is a hallmark of Jim Crow legislation. While the statute does not explicitly mandate segregation within the schools themselves, the discriminatory voting requirement is sufficient to classify it as a Jim Crow law. The confidence is high due to the explicit mention of race in a discriminatory context. The category is 'education' as the statute directly pertains to the establishment and governance of schools.

§ 4483. Assessment and collection of tax—duties of officers. The assessment of property, the collection of taxes, powers and duties of trustees and other officers in graded common school districts, shall be governed by section 4443.

§ 4484. Title to school and seminary property to vest in board—conditions. The title to all common school and all county seminary property, the county court and the board of trustees of said seminary consenting, in the limits of any graded common school district organized under the provisions of this law, shall be, and the same is hereby, vested in the board of trustees of said graded common school district, and they are hereby empowered to sell and convey the same, or to use the same for graded common school purposes, as to them shall seem best; but when county seminary property shall be appropriated, all pupils of the county shall be permitted to attend such school at such reduced tuition from what is ordinary as shall be equitable and make good to them their interest in said seminary property. It is further provided, that when any graded school district shall embrace any school property owned or held in trust by trustees, said trustees, by a majority of their board, are hereby authorized and empowered to convey their school property to the trustees of the graded school, at such price and on such conditions as may be agreed upon by the trustees of both parties. (*Section as amended by act of February 24, 1894.*)

§ 4485. Trustees to appoint officers of election—duty of officers. After the first election provided for in this law shall have been held, the tax voted, trustees elected, and the graded common school organized, the board of trustees shall appoint the officers to hold all other elections, which officers shall take an oath to be under the same responsibilities and subject to the same penalties as the officers holding State or county elections, only they shall make returns of poll-books, and certify the result of the elections to the board of trustees, who shall examine and compare the same and issue certificates to the persons found to be elected.

§ 4486. Tax—election to impose may be held every two years. If it be found that a majority of the votes cast upon the said proposition in the election provided for in section 4464 to be cast against said tax, then the said tax shall not be levied or collected. But the question of voting the said tax may, after the expiration of two years from the first or any subsequent vote, be again submitted to the legal voters of said district upon the conditions and in the manner prescribed for the first vote.

It specifies the interest rate (6% payable semi-annually) and the allocation of the semi-annual interest payment of $4,950 between the two institutions, with $627.75 designated for the State Normal School for Colored Persons and $4,322.25 for the Agricultural and Mechanical College. classification.summary: This statute empowers fiscal courts in Kentucky counties to subscribe to stock in turnpike road companies. It outlines the process for levying taxes to fund these subscriptions, including voter approval, and sets limits on the amount that can be subscribed per mile. The roads are to be maintained for the benefit of the traveling public, with tolls limited to repair and incidental expenses. Alternatively, counties can maintain roads through taxation instead of tolls.
classification.reasoning: The statute concerns the funding and management of turnpike roads by county fiscal courts. It details the process for public subscription to stock in turnpike companies, the levying of taxes to support these investments, and the management of road maintenance and tolls. There is no mention of race, segregation, or any differential treatment based on race. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law.

It requires a majority vote of legal voters in a regular election to approve such an appropriation, provided the funds are not already designated for a specific purpose. It also details the representation of fiscal courts on boards of directors for turnpike companies and the compensation of these directors.

There is no mention of race, nor are there any provisions that implicitly suggest racial segregation or discrimination. The focus is purely on fiscal and administrative matters related to public infrastructure. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law.

classification.summary: This statute outlines the process for a county to hold an election to decide whether to appropriate funds for the building and maintenance of turnpike, gravel, and plank roads. If a majority favors the appropriation, three commissioners are appointed to oversee the road construction, including the power to condemn land and manage funds. The statute also states that general election laws govern these elections.

classification.title: VAGRANTS
classification.summary: This statute outlines the legal process for identifying, trying, and punishing individuals deemed vagrants. Convicted vagrants over twenty-one years of age could be bound out to labor or sold into servitude for up to twelve months. Minors would be apprenticed until the age of twenty-one. The proceeds from the sale of a vagrant were to be used first for prosecution fees, then to pay the vagrant's debts, and any remainder was to be paid to the wife and children, or the vagrant upon completion of their term. Married men with families could be discharged if they posted bond to support their families and engage in honest work. The statute also details the rights and powers of those who purchased or took in a vagrant.
classification.reasoning: The statute addresses vagrancy, which was a category often used to criminalize and control Black individuals after the Civil War. While race is not explicitly mentioned, the practice of 'binding out' or 'selling into servitude' for vagrants, particularly for extended periods, strongly suggests a mechanism that could be used to enforce racial hierarchies and labor control, similar to other Jim Crow era laws. The ambiguity arises because the statute itself doesn't specify race, but its historical context and the nature of the penalties make it highly suspect as a tool of racial oppression. Therefore, human review is needed to confirm its application in a racially discriminatory manner.

classification.title: WORK-HOUSES
classification.summary: This statute, enacted in 1876 and appearing in the 1903 Kentucky Statutes, grants county courts the power to establish and manage work-houses. It outlines the process for acquiring land, constructing facilities, appointing managers, prescribing rules for prisoner labor and conduct, and the possibility of leasing the work-house and prisoner labor for up to one year. The manager is responsible for the safekeeping, feeding, lodging, and medical care of prisoners, as well as ensuring they work according to regulations. The lessee of the work-house assumes similar duties and powers as the manager.
classification.reasoning: The statute details the establishment and operation of county work-houses. It outlines the powers of the county court in managing these institutions, including the appointment of managers, the prescription of rules for prisoners, and the potential leasing of the work-house and prisoner labor. While work-houses were often used to enforce racial segregation and control Black populations during the Jim Crow era, this specific text does not contain any explicit or implicit racial indicators. The language is general and applies to all individuals committed to the work-house, regardless of race. Therefore, it is classified as 'no' for Jim Crow, with a high confidence. The category is 'incarceration' as it directly pertains to correctional facilities. The document type is 'session_laws' as indicated by 'Act of March 9, 1876' and its inclusion in a compiled statute book.
